relationship: a covenant relationship described as broken
rationale: Zechariah's discarded staff symbolizes dissolution of a covenant made with all the peoples. Jeremiah contrasts the promised new covenant with the fathers' failure to remain in the earlier covenant and God's disregard of them. Both describe the breakdown of a covenant relation, while the parties and symbolic action remain distinct.
source_text: I will take my beautiful staff and throw it away, to dissolve my covenant that I made with all the peoples.

target_units.text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,

not according to the covenant I made with their fathers on the day I took their hand to bring them out of Egypt’s land, because they did not remain in My covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

relationship: thirty silver pieces weighed out as a payment
rationale: Zechariah's shepherd receives wages weighed out as thirty silver pieces. Matthew likewise reports thirty silver coins weighed out to Judas when he offers to hand Jesus over. The precise amount and weighed payment connect the passages, without identifying wages and betrayal as the same transaction.
source_text: I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

target_units.text: Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
and said, “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand Him over to you?” They weighed out for him thirty silver coins.
From then on he sought a suitable opportunity to hand Him over.

relationship: a specified payment of thirty in silver
rationale: Zechariah names thirty silver pieces as the shepherd's wages. Exodus specifies thirty didrachmas of silver paid to a slave's master when a bull gores the slave. Both give a thirty-unit silver payment, with their different units and legal or narrative functions preserved.
source_text: I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

target_units.text: And if the bull gores a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty didrachmas of silver to their master, and the bull shall be stoned.

relationship: thirty silver coins thrown into the sacred house with different dispositions
rationale: Zechariah throws thirty silver pieces into the Lord's house, into a smelting furnace. Matthew reports Judas throwing the returned thirty coins into the sanctuary, after which priests buy the potter's field. The temple disposal and sum connect the accounts; furnace and potter's field remain different, and Matthew's quoted attribution to Jeremiah is preserved.
source_text: The Lord said to me, “Put them into the smelting furnace and examine whether it is approved, as I was tested on their behalf.” I took the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the Lord’s house, into the smelting furnace.

target_units.text: Then Judas, who had handed Him over, saw that He had been condemned. Filled with regret, he returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders,
saying, “I sinned by handing over innocent blood.” They said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”
He threw the silver coins into the sanctuary and withdrew; then he went away and hanged himself.
The chief priests took the silver coins and said, “It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, because they are the price of blood.”
After taking counsel, they bought the potter’s field with them as a burial place for strangers.
Therefore that field has been called Field of Blood until today.
Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “They took the thirty silver coins, the price of the One priced, whom some of the sons of Israel priced,
and gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

relationship: contrasting staff actions concerning Judah and Israel
rationale: Zechariah discards Measuring Cord to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel. Ezekiel instead joins staffs representing Judah and Joseph with Israel into one, explaining the end of their division. The symbolic staffs concern the relationship of the named peoples, but the actions and outcomes contrast.
source_text: I threw away the second staff, Measuring Cord, to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel.

target_units.text: ‘Son of man, take a staff for yourself and write upon it Judah and Israel’s sons attached to him. Take a second staff for yourself and write upon it, For Joseph—Ephraim’s staff—and all Israel’s sons joined to him.
Join them to one another for yourself as one staff, binding them together, and they will be in your hand.
When your people’s sons say to you, Will you not tell us what these things mean to you?

say to them, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take Joseph’s tribe through Ephraim’s hand, and Israel’s tribes attached to him, and place them upon Judah’s tribe. They will become one staff in Judah’s hand.
The staffs upon which you wrote will be in your hand before them,

and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

relationship: a shepherd fails to seek, heal and protect the sheep
rationale: Zechariah's coming shepherd neglects failing, scattered, broken and whole sheep and consumes the choice ones. Ezekiel likewise condemns shepherds who slaughter the fattened animal but fail to strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind the broken or seek the lost. The detailed catalogue of neglected care closely corresponds.
source_text: Look, I am raising up a shepherd over the land: he will certainly not attend to what is failing, seek what is scattered, heal what is broken or guide what is whole. He will devour the flesh of the choice ones and wrench their ankle bones.

target_units.text: Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fattened animal, but you do not feed My sheep.
You have not strengthened the weak, restored the sick to health, bound up the broken, brought back the wandering or sought the lost. You have worn down the strong with toil.

relationship: a shepherding figure abandons the sheep
rationale: Zechariah condemns those shepherding worthless things who abandon the sheep. Jesus' comparison likewise depicts a hired worker leaving the sheep and fleeing because he does not care for them. Both identify abandonment as failed care, without transferring the sword punishment to John's worker.
source_text: Oh, you who shepherd worthless things and have abandoned the sheep! A sword against his arms and his right eye! His arm will utterly wither, and his right eye will be completely blinded.”

target_units.text: The hired worker, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees—and the wolf seizes them and scatters them—
because he is a hired worker and does not care for the sheep.

relationship: the Creator of heaven and earth gives human spirit
rationale: Zechariah introduces the Lord as stretching heaven, founding earth and forming the human spirit. Isaiah likewise names Him as maker of heaven, establisher of earth and giver of breath and spirit to people. The threefold creator description closely corresponds.
source_text: An oracle of the Lord’s word concerning Israel. The Lord says—He who stretches out heaven, founds earth and forms a person’s spirit within him:

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord God, who made heaven and fixed it in place, established the earth and its contents, and gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those treading it:

relationship: Jerusalem surrounded and besieged
rationale: Zechariah announces siege against Jerusalem alongside its shaking-entranceways image. Isaiah likewise describes a surrounding palisade and towers and names nations marching against Jerusalem. The connection concerns the explicitly besieged city, without replacing Zechariah's image with a cup.
source_text: “Look, I am making Jerusalem like shaking entranceways for all the peoples around, and in Judea there will be a siege against Jerusalem.

target_units.text: I will surround you like David, set a palisade around you and set towers around you,
and your words will be humbled into the earth and sink into the earth. Your voice will be like those who speak from the earth, and your voice will weaken toward the ground.
The wealth of the ungodly will be like dust from a wheel, like drifting chaff, and it will be like a moment, immediately,
from the Lord Sabaoth. For there will be a visitation with thunder, earthquake and a great sound, a rushing storm and a consuming flame of fire.
Like someone dreaming in sleep will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Ariel, all who marched against Jerusalem, and all assembled against her and afflicting her.

relationship: hostile nations gathered against Zion
rationale: Zechariah says all earth's nations gather against Jerusalem. Micah likewise describes many nations gathered against Zion, rejoicing over her without understanding the Lord's purpose. Both present the hostile gathering around the named city, without importing injury to stone-lifters into Zechariah's trampled stone.
source_text: On that day I will make Jerusalem a trampled stone for all the nations. Everyone trampling her will mock in mockery, and all the earth’s nations will gather against her.

target_units.text: Now many nations have gathered against you, saying, “We will rejoice over her, and our eyes will look upon Zion!”
But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

relationship: the Lord strikes with madness, blindness and bewilderment
rationale: Zechariah announces bewildered horses, maddened riders and blind horses among the peoples. Deuteronomy likewise names madness, blindness and mental bewilderment among the Lord's blows. The unusual cluster connects the warnings, with different recipients.
source_text: On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness. Over Judah’s house I will open My eyes, and I will strike all the peoples’ horses with blindness.

target_units.text: The Lord smite you with madness, and with blindness, and with bewilderment of mind.

relationship: God's people pictured as fire consuming opposing peoples
rationale: Zechariah likens Judah's commanders to a firebrand and flaming torch consuming surrounding peoples. Obadiah likewise pictures Jacob as fire, Joseph as flame and Esau as stubble consumed by them. Both use fire for the people overcoming opponents, while those opponents differ.
source_text: On that day I will make Judah’s commanders of thousands like a firebrand among wood and a flaming torch among stalks. They will consume all the surrounding peoples to right and left, and Jerusalem will again dwell by herself.

target_units.text: The house of Jacob will be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble. They will blaze against them and consume them, and there will be no bearer of fire in the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.

relationship: the weak become strong in a battle setting
rationale: Zechariah promises divine shielding so that the weak among Jerusalem's residents become like David's house. Joel likewise calls the powerless strong and the meek a fighter in the setting of gathered nations. Both express transformed weakness through battle strength, without equating all the participants.
source_text: On that day the Lord will shield Jerusalem’s residents. The weak among them will be like David’s house on that day, and David’s house like God’s house, like the angel of the Lord before them.

target_units.text: Beat your plows into swords and your sickles into lances; let the powerless say, “I am strong!”
Assemble and enter, all surrounding nations, and gather there! Let the meek become a fighter!

relationship: the hostile gathering against Jerusalem is frustrated
rationale: Zechariah promises the Lord's removal of nations coming against Jerusalem. Isaiah describes the wealth of all nations marching against Jerusalem and Zion as a futile dream. Both overturn the hostile assembly's expected success through different images.
source_text: On that day I will seek to remove all the nations coming against Jerusalem.

target_units.text: Like someone dreaming in sleep will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Ariel, all who marched against Jerusalem, and all assembled against her and afflicting her.

They will be like people drinking and eating in sleep; when they rise, their dream is futile. As a thirsty person dreams of drinking but wakes still thirsty, his soul having hoped in vain, so will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Mount Zion.

relationship: God promises an outpouring of spirit
rationale: Zechariah promises pouring a spirit of grace and compassion upon David's house and Jerusalem's residents. Joel likewise promises pouring out of God's Spirit upon all flesh, including slaves. Both expressly announce an outpouring, while recipients and stated effects differ.
source_text: I will pour upon David’s house and Jerusalem’s residents a spirit of grace and compassion. They will look toward Me because they danced in mockery, and mourn over him as over a beloved one; they will suffer grief as over a firstborn.

target_units.text: “And it shall be after these things, that I will pour out of My Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your elders shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.
Even upon male slaves and female slaves in those days I will pour out of My Spirit.

relationship: mourning compared with grief for a beloved one
rationale: Zechariah describes mourning over someone as over a beloved one and grief as over a firstborn. Jeremiah likewise commands the daughter of the people to make a pitiful lament for a beloved one. The particular comparison of grief connects the passages without inserting piercing into Zechariah's mockery wording.
source_text: I will pour upon David’s house and Jerusalem’s residents a spirit of grace and compassion. They will look toward Me because they danced in mockery, and mourn over him as over a beloved one; they will suffer grief as over a firstborn.

target_units.text: Daughter of My people, gird yourself with sackcloth; sprinkle yourself with ashes. Make mourning for yourself for a beloved one, a pitiful lament, because misery will suddenly come upon you.

relationship: the removal and forgetting of idols' names
rationale: Zechariah promises destruction of idols' names and the end of their remembrance. Hosea likewise promises removing the Baalim's names from the woman's mouth so they will no longer be remembered. Both explicitly remove the names as well as their remembrance.
source_text: On that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the idols’ names from the land, and there will no longer be remembrance of them. I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.

target_units.text: I will remove the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and they will certainly no longer remember their names.

relationship: a false prophet speaking in the Lord's name is declared liable to death
rationale: Zechariah's parents tell their prophesying child he must not live because he spoke falsehood in the Lord's name. Deuteronomy likewise declares death for a prophet speaking in God's name words not commanded. The offense and stated consequence correspond; Zechariah subsequently describes binding feet rather than narrating execution.
source_text: If a person still prophesies, his father and mother who begot him will say to him, ‘You shall not live, because you spoke falsehoods in the Lord’s name.’ His father and mother who begot him will bind his feet when he prophesies.

target_units.text: But the prophet who shall act ungodly, speaking in My name a word which I commanded him not to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die.

relationship: family allegiance does not excuse religious deception
rationale: Zechariah depicts parents opposing their own child for false prophecy in the Lord's name. Deuteronomy likewise prohibits protecting even close relatives who entice someone to other gods. Both place rejection of religious deception above family protection, while the offenses and prescribed actions differ.
source_text: If a person still prophesies, his father and mother who begot him will say to him, ‘You shall not live, because you spoke falsehoods in the Lord’s name.’ His father and mother who begot him will bind his feet when he prophesies.

target_units.text: And if your brother, the son of your father or of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying: Let us go and serve other gods, which you have not known, you nor your fathers,
of the gods of the nations round about you, whether near unto you or far from you, from one end of the earth unto the other,
you shall not consent unto him, neither shall you hearken unto him; neither shall your eye spare him, nor shall you yearn for him, nor conceal him.
You shall surely report him; your hands shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people.
And they shall stone him with stones, and he shall die; for he sought to turn you away from the Lord your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

relationship: false visions expose prophets to judgment
rationale: Zechariah describes prophets ashamed of their visions and explicitly says they lied. Ezekiel likewise confronts false visions and vain divinations and announces the prophets' exclusion from Israel's register and land. Both condemn the false visionary claim without assigning Zechariah's hairy skin to Ezekiel.
source_text: On that day the prophets will be ashamed, each because of his vision when he prophesies; they will wear a hairy skin because they lied.

target_units.text: Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations?
Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations vain, therefore behold, I am against you, says the Lord,

and I will stretch out My hand against the prophets who see false things and utter vain things. They will not belong to My people’s instruction, nor be written in the register of the house of Israel, nor enter Israel’s land. They will know that I am the Lord.
